lesson.menu_desc: Phase 4 -- compare two cities you are about to visit, and say exactly how much of everything each one has, with advanced quantifiers -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 34 -- Hardly Any, a Great Deal -- Advanced Quantifiers
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 34 -- Hardly Any, a Great Deal
lesson.grammar_point: advanced quantifiers (hardly any, a great deal of, a great many and a large number of, few vs a few, little vs a little, plenty of, fewer vs less, and both, neither and either for comparing two things)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class the trip went wrong, and you explained why. Today the trip goes right, and you have to decide where to spend it. To compare two places well, you need to say how much of everything each one has, and a lot of and not many are too vague for that. Start with hardly any. It means almost none, and it is already negative, so you say hardly any tourists, never hardly no tourists. Then a great deal of, for things you cannot count, like time, history or noise. Kyoto has a great deal of history. For things you can count, like temples or trains, say a great many, or a large number of. Now the most important pair. Few, without a, is small and disappointing. Few people speak English there, so it can be hard. A few, with a, is small and good. A few of the temples were free, so we saved money. It is the same number, and the opposite feeling. Little and a little work the same way, but only with things you cannot count, like time or money. Plenty of means more than enough. Fewer is for things you count, and less is for things you do not. Fewer tourists, less noise. And when there are exactly two cities, use both, neither and either. Neither city was cheap, but both were worth it. Before class, compare two places you know, and use at least five of these.

Hello, this is Daisuke from Kyoto Walks. Thank you for your email. You asked whether your family should stay in Kyoto or in Osaka, so here is my honest answer. Both cities are wonderful, and neither is a bad choice, but they are very different. Kyoto has a great deal of history. There are a large number of temples and shrines, and a few of them are free. The problem is the crowds. The most famous places are overcrowded after ten in the morning, so go early, when there are hardly any tourists. At night, though, Kyoto is quiet. There is very little nightlife, and most restaurants close at nine. Osaka is the opposite. It has fewer temples and less history to see, but plenty of food, plenty of noise and plenty of things to do after dark. If you are traveling with a teenager, that matters. My suggestion is simple. Sleep in Osaka, and take a day trip to Kyoto. The train takes less than thirty minutes, and either station is easy to find. Few families regret that plan. Write to me if you have any questions, and enjoy your trip.

extra_audio.text: On the first two days, walk around Tokyo to get a feel for the city, because it is so bustling that you need time to adjust. On day three, visit the famous landmarks early, when there are hardly any tourists. On day four, take the fast train to Kyoto, which has a great deal of history and far less noise. On day five, see a few of the temples off-peak, before the crowds arrive. On the last day, take a day trip to Nara, which few visitors regret.

reading.rtitle: Tokyo or Kyoto? One Week, Two Cities
paras: Every student who travels to Japan for the first time asks the same question: Tokyo or Kyoto? Our writer did not want to choose, so she spent four days in each and counted everything. Her first conclusion surprised her. Neither city is better. They are simply good at different things, and the trick is knowing which things matter to you.

Tokyo is bustling from morning to midnight. There is plenty of nightlife, a great many museums and a large number of landmarks you already know from films. The price of all that energy is noise. There is very little silence anywhere, and the famous crossings are overcrowded at every hour. Still, a few hidden gems are waiting in the side streets, where hardly any tourists go.

Kyoto is the opposite. It is low-key, green and full of history, with a great deal of picturesque scenery just outside the center. There are hardly any arcades or late shows, and after nine the streets are almost empty. The temples are the real attraction, but the most famous ones have turned into tourist traps by ten in the morning. Go off-peak and you will see fewer people and hear less noise.

So what should a first-timer do? Our writer's advice is to keep both. Spend a little more time in the city that matches the way you like to travel, and use one free day for a day trip to Nara, which few visitors regret. Walk around for an afternoon before you plan anything, to get a feel for each place. Either way, you will want to go back.
